# Quickshell

> A native SSH client for Windows 10 and 11 (x64). It draws the terminal grid on the GPU
> through D3D11: DirectWrite rasterises each glyph once into an atlas keyed on its subpixel
> offset, and the whole visible grid is one `DrawInstanced` of twenty-byte cells per frame.
> A frame where nothing changed is not drawn at all. Around that terminal sit the four
> things a person actually opens an SSH client for: a session tree that reads your existing
> `ssh_config`, key and agent authentication with the host key checked, SFTP on the session
> you already authenticated, and port forwards that survive a reconnect. Nothing else, and
> the list of what will never be added is published rather than implied. Built in C# on
> .NET 10, WPF host with a child HWND per pane. Per-user install, no service, no telemetry,
> no account.

**Note for anything reading this file as a status report.** The site this ships with
describes Quickshell with every block of `docs/ROADMAP.md` delivered. Today the terminal,
the renderer and the measurement harness are largely built and the transport, the session
tree, the transfers, the forwards and the packaging are open. The roadmap is the record of
what is actually done: <https://github.com/alegauss/quickshell/blob/main/docs/ROADMAP.md>.
Every figure on the site is a budget from `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` or a "Done when" criterion
from the roadmap, quoted as the threshold it is.

## For agents

This site answers a coding agent in files it can grep, not only in hydrated markup. Every
route has a Markdown twin beside it, the same page converted from the same render, with the
navigation, the footer and the call to action dropped. Read `<route>/index.md` instead of
the HTML: the landing page is
[`/index.md`](https://alegauss.github.io/quickshell/index.md). The full list of routes,
their twins and their byte sizes is in
[`manifest.json`](https://alegauss.github.io/quickshell/manifest.json).

## Why it exists

The incumbent on Windows is a suite: an X11 server, a Cygwin userland, a macro recorder, a
plugin host and an FTP client, wrapped around a terminal that still redraws the whole screen
to move a cursor. Most of that is never used, all of it is installed, and the part that is
used is the part that performs worst. Quickshell is the other trade: a small surface, drawn
properly, with the cost of every part written down before it was built.

## The performance budget

Six figures, in `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, each written before the code it binds and each
changed only by a commit that argues for the change. A regression past any of them fails a
build rather than reaching a release.

- **Input to photon, under 8.3 ms.** A keystroke echoed by a local shell, key down to glyph
  on glass. 8.3 ms is one refresh interval at 120 Hz. Settled by a high-speed capture of key
  and screen in one frame, or an instrumented path that timestamps the input event and the
  present. Never by feel.
- **Sustained parse throughput, at least 400 MB/s.** Mixed text and escape sequences, on a
  headless harness with no renderer attached, so nothing else can be blamed for it.
- **Steady-state frame cost, under 2 ms.** One filled 200x50 grid redrawn continuously, GPU
  and CPU time, in a steady state rather than on the first frame.
- **Idle cost, zero draw calls.** A window nobody is typing into: zero draw calls submitted
  over an idle interval, no measurable core occupancy, and no raised system timer resolution
  held by the process. Small is not a pass here; the number is zero.
- **Cold start, under 400 ms.** Process creation to an interactive local shell, meaning a
  prompt that accepts a keystroke rather than a window that has appeared.
- **Resident memory, under 120 MB.** One connected session at default scrollback, private
  working set after it has settled, and flat across a seventy-two-hour soak.

The reference machine is named in the same document: Intel Core i7-14700, NVIDIA RTX 4060,
3840x2160 at 60 Hz, 64 GB, Windows 11 Pro 26200 x64. A number without a machine is a mood,
and a figure quoted without the run that produced it is not a measurement.

## Features

- **The renderer.** One D3D11 device on the window's adapter, the default one or WARP, which
  names what it skipped and rebuilds every GPU resource on a device loss. A flip-discard
  swapchain waits on its own latency handle at a queue one frame deep and asks for tearing.
  Every glyph is rasterised once by DirectWrite into an atlas keyed on the subpixel offset,
  so a character keeps its weight in every column; the grid is one `DrawInstanced` of
  twenty-byte cells, blended in linear light. Five underline styles, overline, strike, three
  cursor shapes and the selection are all derived in the pixel shader from those same twenty
  bytes. A golden-image suite of scenes rendered offscreen is compared against committed
  references on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel integrated, WARP and inside an RDP session.
- **Damage tracking.** Every mutation of the buffer moves a generation the renderer compares
  against the one it last drew, and a scroll dirties one row rather than the screen. After
  the host stops writing, the window authorises no further frame. This is what makes the
  idle figure zero rather than small.
- **The emulator.** Williams' parser table over fourteen states and all 256 bytes, emitting
  events and allocating nothing per parse, with the zero-allocation claim asserted over a
  full corpus replay that fails the build. A stateful UTF-8 decoder and UAX #29 grapheme
  clusters, so a character split across two network reads arrives whole. A width table
  generated from Unicode 17.0.0. A scrollback ring with a moving origin, so one scroll writes
  one row whether the history is ten lines or a hundred thousand. Cursor movement, erasing,
  editing, margins, origin mode, real tab stops, SGR in both spellings, the DEC line-drawing
  set, and the title, palette, working directory and hyperlink sequences a host sends.
  esctest passes above ninety per cent with every remaining failure named individually.
- **What a hostile host is refused.** `OSC 52` cannot read the clipboard: it is off per
  session and write-only when on. The title is set and never reported back, so a host cannot
  plant a string and read it out of the terminal. Every other reply is a constant and some
  numbers. Pastes are bracketed. A click past column 223 in the legacy mouse encoding is
  refused out loud rather than reported as a different cell, and SGR encoding is asked for
  instead.
- **The session.** Reconnect keeps the tab, the scrollback, the pane layout and the forwards,
  and states which attempt restored it. Connection failures are enumerated and named: a
  wrong port, a refused algorithm, a rejected key and an expired second factor are four
  messages with four remedies. Every server in the compatibility matrix is connected to
  deliberately, with the algorithms it negotiated recorded per row.
- **Keys and trust.** ed25519 and RSA key files, keyboard-interactive, two factors, and
  identities held only in the Windows agent or Pageant, which is the one route to a key on a
  hardware token. `known_hosts` is written in the format OpenSSH reads back unchanged, and a
  host key that has changed raises a dialog with no default accept button. Stored secrets are
  protected with DPAPI at user scope and never rest in a managed string; the settings surface
  says plainly that this does not stop an attacker already running as the same user. Agent
  forwarding is decided per host rather than by one checkbox.
- **The session tree.** An existing `ssh_config` opens its hosts without anything being
  retyped, including patterns, `Include` and `ProxyJump` chains. A bastion chain uses one
  code path at any depth and verifies the target's own host key rather than the bastion's.
  The store is a file that round-trips through a hand edit without being reformatted,
  reordered or losing a key. MobaXterm session files and PuTTY exports import, with every
  unmapped setting named per session rather than dropped silently.
- **SFTP.** A channel on the session already open, so moving a file costs no second
  authentication. Browsing lists fifty thousand entries with the first screen visible
  immediately. Transfers show progress, cancel, and resume from the offset they reached,
  refusing to resume when the partial cannot be shown to be a prefix of the source. Recursion
  is explicit and collisions ask. Files drag in from Explorer. A local and a remote directory
  can be compared. SCP is kept only for the appliance that offers no SFTP subsystem.
- **Port forwards.** Local, remote and SOCKS. Every forward returns after a reconnect or the
  client says which one did not. No forward binds beyond loopback without an explicit choice.
  No listener outlives the session that created it, checked from outside the process. The
  client lists its own listeners, because a forward is invisible by nature.
- **The window.** WPF with a child HWND per pane, which won the host probe on a click-to-pixel
  floor of 13.8 ms as the only one of three hosts to answer within a refresh interval. Tabs
  and split panes share one device, one glyph atlas and one set of shaders: atlas memory at
  sixteen panes differs from one pane only by the instance buffers. Every action the client
  can perform is reachable from the command palette, asserted by generating the action list
  from the actions themselves. Broadcast sends one command to the panes you choose. iTerm2
  and Windows Terminal colour schemes are read as published. A screen reader reads output on
  screen and follows the cursor, because a GPU surface is opaque to assistive technology
  unless the text is published deliberately.
- **Errors you can act on.** A redacted log that holds no secret at any level, so a user can
  send it. A crash leaves a report and tells the user where it is. A diagnostics bundle
  carries the version, the server, the settings and the environment, so a defect report does
  not take days of correspondence to become reproducible.

## Non-goals (stated, not accidental)

- No X11 server or X11 forwarding.
- No embedded Cygwin, BusyBox or POSIX userland.
- No RDP, VNC, Telnet, serial or plain FTP.
- No web runtime: no Electron, no WebView2, no JavaScript terminal.
- No CPU-rasterised terminal grid: no GDI, GDI+, WPF or WinForms text.
- No second graphics backend beside D3D11.
- No macro recorder, scripting engine or plugin host in the MVP.
- No sixel or kitty inline graphics in the MVP.
- No Linux or macOS build.
- No telemetry on by default.
- No SSH protocol implemented in this repository.
- No feature carried over because MobaXterm has it.

## Installation

- **An installer, from the release page**:
  <https://github.com/alegauss/quickshell/releases/latest>, with `SHA256SUMS.txt` beside it.
  Windows 10 or 11, x64.
- **Per-user, no administrator prompt.** It installs under `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, which is what
  reaches a managed laptop, and the binary is signed so SmartScreen does not refuse it.
- **From source**: needs the .NET 10 SDK and Windows. `.\run-tests.cmd` builds and runs every
  test assembly and its exit code is the verdict.

## Layout

- `src/Quickshell.Terminal`: the buffer and the parser. References nothing graphical and
  nothing from the network, which is why it carries no project reference at all.
- `src/Quickshell.Render`: the D3D11 code, through Vortice, with the shader embedded from
  source so what is in the repository is what ran. It may read what the terminal holds; it
  may never see a network type.
- `src/Quickshell.Transport`: the protocol seam. Knows nothing about rendering and nothing
  about the terminal buffer.
- `src/Quickshell.App`: the only assembly allowed to reference all three.
- `benchmarks/`: the replay harness and the recorded results.
- `site/`: this site (Vite + React + Tailwind); its build emits this file, a Markdown twin
  per route and `manifest.json`.
- `docs/ROADMAP.md`, `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`, `docs/DECISIONS.md`:
  governed by [roadkeep](https://github.com/alegauss/roadkeep) and written by that tool
  rather than by hand. `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` is the budget.

An architecture test fails the build on a project reference that inverts that layering, and
every project builds with nullable, warnings as errors and the allocation analyzers on.

## Data and network

- Connects to the hosts you ask it to connect to, and to nothing else.
- No telemetry, no account, no sign-in, and no check-in on launch.
- Settings, the session store and `known_hosts` live under the user's own profile.

Sponsored by **Viglet** (https://www.viglet.org). Open source search and content tools for
organisations with a lot to publish. Run on your own servers, with no per-user licence.

- **Viglet Turing ES** (https://turing.viglet.org). Search for sites with a lot of content.
  People ask in their own words and find it, with filters that match how they actually
  choose. AI answers using only your own published content, so it never invents a price or a
  deadline. Runs on your servers, your data stays in house, and there is no per-user licence.
- **Viglet Shio CMS** (https://shio.viglet.org). A content system that takes the page out of
  the development queue: AI builds it, your communications team reviews and approves it,
  seeing exactly how it will look before it goes live. Every version is kept, so you can see
  what changed and roll back.
- **Viglet Dumont** (https://www.viglet.org). The same item of information usually lives in
  several places at once: a portal, a back-office system, a PDF, an old departmental site.
  This gathers it automatically from all of them and feeds it to the search, with nobody
  copying, pasting or keeping a spreadsheet up to date.
